claim: Give your primary/accent colour one fixed semantic job across every dialog in the product — most commonly 'this is the safe, non-destructive action' — and never let it mark a destructive action anywhere.
why: Users stop reading dialog copy after a few encounters and start acting on colour position alone; a colour that means the same thing every time turns into a reliable shortcut, while one exception makes the whole signal untrustworthy and causes data loss.
when: Any confirmation, destructive-action, or multi-button dialog in a product users will encounter repeatedly.
fails: Breaks if some dialogs legitimately need the destructive path to be the default action; in those cases the destructive option needs its own reserved treatment rather than borrowing the primary colour, otherwise the learned rule is inverted at the worst moment.

claim: Apply the same button sizing and spacing, type scale, and colour roles across screens with completely unrelated purposes — a settings panel and a creation flow should be visually indistinguishable at the component level.
why: Consistency across unrelated contexts is what proves the system is a system; when only related screens match, users still have to re-learn each area of the product.
when: Any product with multiple distinct surfaces, panels, or sections built by the same team.

claim: Build a new screen by assembling components and spacing values that already exist in the product, and only design something new when no existing decision covers the need.
why: If the system is real, most new screens are a recombination problem, not a design problem — which is why new surfaces become fast to produce and instantly familiar to users.
when: Adding screens, modals, or flows to a product that already has an established component set.
fails: Misapplied when a genuinely new interaction is forced into an ill-fitting existing component just to preserve consistency; the system should be extended in that case, not stretched.

claim: Structure creation modals in a fixed vertical order: shortcut or template selection at the top, then input fields in order of importance (title before description before optional metadata like tags), then the action buttons anchored at the bottom.
why: A repeated skeleton means users locate the confirm button and the primary field by position rather than by reading, and the fastest path (start from a template) is offered before the slowest one (fill everything manually).
when: Modals or panels where the user is creating a new object with several fields.

claim: Optimise for a short list of decisions you enforce everywhere rather than a large library of components — a system with ten rules that are never broken beats one with a hundred components applied inconsistently.
why: The value users receive comes from predictability, and predictability is produced by adherence, not by inventory size; a large library with exceptions delivers no learnable pattern.
when: Deciding how much design-system infrastructure a product actually needs, especially on small teams or early products.

claim: Validate a newly designed screen by placing it side by side with existing screens of the same class and checking that it reads as part of the same family despite different content.
why: Familiarity is the observable output of a working system, so a direct visual comparison is a cheap test of whether the new screen actually inherited the decisions or quietly invented new ones.
when: Reviewing any new surface before it ships.

claim: Treat the design system as the third layer on top of user flows and realistic content — apply it only after the flow and the real data are settled.
why: A consistent visual language applied to an unresolved flow or placeholder content just makes a bad structure look tidy; the system's job is to make a correct structure legible and repeatable.
when: Sequencing product design work end to end.

claim: Pick one corner-radius value for all small components (buttons, inputs, chips, tags) and apply it everywhere — around 10px works as a default for mobile-scale UI.
why: Radius is a silent signature; when it varies element to element the eye registers the drift as sloppiness even when nothing else is wrong.
when: Any screen containing multiple small interactive elements, especially mobile app UI at typical control heights of 40–56px.
fails: Deliberate radius tiers are a legitimate system choice — e.g. small controls at one radius, cards or sheets at a larger one, pills at fully rounded. The rule is one value per size tier, not one value for the entire product.

claim: When two elements do the same kind of job (a back button and a skip button, two search fields), make them identical in size, corner radius, fill, border, and type style, and let only the content differ.
why: Visual difference is a signal; if two controls look different, users read them as behaving differently. Identical roles rendered differently spend that signal on nothing.
when: Paired or sibling controls appearing in the same screen or the same slot across a flow — nav actions, form fields, list rows, onboarding footers.
fails: The controls genuinely differ in priority — a primary and a secondary action should share geometry but intentionally differ in fill and weight to express hierarchy.

claim: Encode consistency in the file rather than reproducing it by hand: colour styles for every fill and stroke, named variables/tokens for spacing and sizing numbers, and components for any UI element used more than once.
why: Hand-copied values drift the moment the design changes; tokenised values propagate a fix from one edit to every instance.
when: Any design file expected to grow past a couple of screens or be handed to another designer or an engineer.
fails: Early exploratory sketching, where premature tokenisation slows down the search for a direction — componentise once the direction is settled.

claim: Audit for consistency by scanning one property at a time across the whole design — all radii, then all spacing, then all text sizes — instead of reviewing screen by screen.
why: Drift is only visible when like is compared with like; reviewing a screen in isolation hides that its button radius disagrees with the button two screens back.
when: Cleanup or polish passes on a design that was built screen by screen.

claim: Treat inconsistency as the first thing to fix in a rough design, before adding new features or visual detail.
why: It is among the cheapest defects to repair and among the largest contributors to work reading as beginner-level, so it has the highest polish-per-minute return.
when: Reviewing or salvaging a design that feels unpolished without an obvious cause.

claim: Give repeated list or card items a leading icon instead of text alone, so the item can be identified by shape before it is read.
why: Icons are recognised faster than words; forcing users to read every card slows scanning and browsing.
when: Grids or lists of comparable items — recipe cards, product tiles, settings rows — where users scan many items to pick one.
fails: When the distinguishing information is genuinely textual (names, dates, prices) and no icon maps to it; a decorative icon then adds noise without aiding recognition.

claim: Replace text-only micro-actions like 'Save' with a recognised icon when the action is standard and space-constrained.
why: An icon occupies less room and reads faster than a word for actions users already know.
when: Secondary utility actions on cards or list rows — save, share, favourite, more.
fails: Primary or destructive actions, or actions with no conventional glyph, where a word is safer than a guessable symbol.

claim: Source every icon in a product from a single icon family so fill style, stroke weight, and corner radius match across the interface.
why: Mixed fill/line treatments and differing stroke weights read as unresolved craft and break the visual rhythm of a screen.
when: Any screen where icons from different origins have accumulated — mixing a filled glyph next to a hairline outline one.
fails: When one library lacks a needed concept; better to draw the missing icon in the house style than to import a foreign one.

claim: When picking from a large icon marketplace, filter by category plus stroke weight and corner style before downloading, rather than searching icon by icon.
why: Search-by-keyword returns visually unrelated icons from many authors; filtering by drawing attributes is what actually guarantees a consistent set.
when: Sourcing icons from an aggregator site rather than a single curated set.

claim: Download and place icons as SVG, not raster images.
why: Vector icons stay crisp at any size and remain recolourable and restylable in the design tool.
when: Any icon brought into a design file or shipped to a front end.

claim: Leave icons unlabelled only when the metaphor is near-universal — home, bookmark, profile, search; give every other icon a label or a tooltip.
why: Well-known glyphs are already decoded by users, but novel or abstract ones become a guessing game that hurts first-run comprehension.
when: Icon-only navigation bars, toolbars, and action rows.
fails: On touch interfaces, where hover tooltips never appear — those need visible labels, long-press hints, or an onboarding pass instead.

claim: Attach a hover tooltip to ambiguous icons rather than adding visible text labels to all of them.
why: It preserves the compactness of an icon-only row while removing the ambiguity for new users, mainly during onboarding.
when: Desktop or pointer-driven interfaces with a mix of obvious and non-obvious icons in one cluster.
fails: Touch-only contexts, or when the icon is so obscure that even experienced users would need the tooltip every time — that argues for a visible label.

claim: Do not invent unusual metaphors for common actions; prefer the conventional glyph users have already learned elsewhere.
why: Novel icons carry no learned meaning, so each one adds interpretation cost.
when: Choosing icons for standard actions across an interface.

claim: Different icon styles may coexist in one product provided each style is confined to its own spatial zone and functional role — one style for navigation, another for content categories, another for item metadata.
why: Consistency is judged locally, within a visual grouping; separation by both position and purpose makes the style shift read as a deliberate system rather than a mismatch.
when: Larger products where nav chrome, content taxonomy, and item-level data have distinct visual jobs.
fails: When the styles appear side by side in the same cluster, or when the same concept is drawn in two styles in different places — then it reads as inconsistency, not hierarchy.

claim: Audit icons as a system, not one at a time: scan a whole screen for icons that are absent, inconsistent, or unexplained before adjusting any single glyph.
why: Icon problems only become visible in aggregate — a single icon looks fine until you see it next to five others drawn differently.
when: Reviewing an existing interface that has grown over time.

claim: Before designing additional dashboard pages, classify each region as a list/table, card, input, or tab, and reuse the pattern you already built for that category rather than inventing new layout.
why: Dashboard surfaces are combinatorially large but structurally repetitive; a fixed component vocabulary makes every new page an assembly job instead of a design job.
when: Expanding a dashboard beyond its first fully designed page, or auditing an existing one for inconsistency.
fails: Highly bespoke surfaces — canvas editors, maps, timelines, onboarding flows — that are not tabular, card-like, or form-like and get distorted if forced into the taxonomy.

claim: Make list rows scannable by choosing exactly one separation mechanism — whitespace, a divider rule, or an alternating/tinted background — rather than stacking two or three of them.
why: Each mechanism already communicates the row boundary; combining them spends visual weight on information the reader has already received and makes the list feel noisy.
when: Any vertically repeating set of items: link lists, sidebar nav, activity feeds, settings rows.
fails: Very wide rows with many columns, where a divider plus generous padding both earn their place because the eye has to travel far horizontally.

claim: Prefer whitespace separation for short, low-density lists and escalate to dividers, then to background fills, as row count and row density increase.
why: Space alone stops reading as a boundary once rows are numerous or tall; a harder edge is needed to keep the eye tracking the correct row.
when: Choosing among the three separation options for a specific list.

claim: Ship every data table with search, column sorting, and at least one filter; treat a table without them as incomplete rather than as a finished simple version.
why: Rendering rows only serves users who want the whole set; the actual job is usually finding a subset, so the controls are what convert a static readout into a working tool.
when: Any table whose row count can grow past a single screen in real usage.
fails: Fixed, short tables — a three-row pricing comparison or a summary breakdown — where controls add chrome with nothing to operate on.

claim: Give card interiors generous internal padding so content never touches the card edge, and keep that padding value consistent across every card in the dashboard.
why: Cards read as discrete objects only if there is a visible air gap inside the boundary; inconsistent padding makes a grid of cards look misaligned even when the outer bounds line up.
when: Any card-based layout: chart tiles, stat panels, toasts, grouped settings blocks.

claim: Define a card boundary with either a border or a background fill, not both, and apply that one choice uniformly across the product.
why: Border and fill are two solutions to the same problem of separating the card from the page; using both doubles the visual weight of every container edge.
when: Establishing the container style in a design system.
fails: Elevated or floating surfaces such as modals, dropdowns, and toasts, which often need a fill plus a hairline border to hold up against varied content behind them.

claim: In dark themes, separate cards with a thin border on a near-flat background; in light themes, separate them with a subtly tinted or white fill against a grey page.
why: Lighter-than-background fills carry poorly in dark mode where the usable luminance range above the page colour is narrow, while in light mode a soft fill separates more gently than a hard line.
when: Setting container conventions for a theme, as a starting default to deviate from deliberately.
fails: Treated as a rule rather than a convention — the source frames it as personal taste, and a strong brand or accessibility target can justify the opposite.

claim: Use tabs to add page-level destinations that belong to the current object, instead of adding another top-level entry to the sidebar.
why: Sidebar length is the main cost driver of navigational overload; tabs buy extra surface area while keeping the user anchored in the same context.
when: Related views of the same underlying data — table views, an entity's overview/activity/settings, grouped configuration panels.
fails: Content that is genuinely a separate destination, or tab sets that grow past roughly five to seven items and start needing their own navigation.

claim: Compose the four component types by nesting them — forms inside cards, cards and lists inside modals, tables inside tabs — rather than treating each as a page-level layout that owns the full width.
why: The categories are building blocks, not templates; complex real surfaces like settings dialogs are just nested combinations of the same four primitives.
when: Designing a dense surface that resists a single flat layout, such as a settings modal or an entity detail page.
fails: Deep nesting where a card sits inside a card inside a modal, at which point the boundaries stop meaning anything.

claim: When switching between related views of the same dataset, keep the user on the page and swap the view via tabs instead of navigating away and back.
why: Preserving page context preserves the user's scroll position, filters, and mental model of where they are.
when: Multiple presentations of one collection — board, table, calendar, gallery.

claim: Match icon box size to the line height of the text it sits beside — if body text runs at a 24px line height, render the icon at 24px.
why: An icon set to the line height occupies exactly one line box, so its optical mass matches the text and the pair reads as a single horizontal unit instead of an image with a label attached.
when: Any icon paired inline with text: nav items, list rows, button labels, menu entries, form field affixes.
fails: Icons meant to carry meaning on their own — empty-state art, feature cards, oversized display icons — where the icon is the content and should be sized independently of any caption.

claim: Default icon sizes from icon libraries are usually too big for inline use; resize deliberately rather than dropping them in as-is.
why: Icon sets ship at generic sizes that were never calibrated to your type scale, so the default reads oversized and pulls attention away from the label.
when: Importing icons from any third-party set into a text-led interface.

claim: After shrinking an icon to line-height size, close the gap between icon and label so the two sit as one tight unit.
why: The spacing that looked correct next to an oversized icon becomes excessive once the icon shrinks; proximity is what binds the pair into a single scannable element.
when: Whenever you resize an icon inside an existing icon-plus-label layout.

claim: Build sidebar and nav links as button components with a transparent background that only fills in on hover, rather than as styled text links.
why: Treating them as buttons gives you a consistent hit area, padding, and state model across the whole nav, and the transparent resting state keeps a long list of items visually quiet.
when: Vertical navigation, sidebars, menu lists, toolbars — any repeated set of clickable rows.
fails: Inline links inside running prose, where a padded button-shaped hit area breaks the text flow and should stay as underlined text.

claim: Treat the ghost button (transparent fill, visible only on hover) as the standard low-emphasis button variant in your button component, alongside filled and outlined.
why: It gives you a third emphasis level that reads as interactive without competing with the primary action, and it's the same component you already use for nav rows.
when: Secondary and tertiary actions, nav items, icon-only toolbar controls, dismiss/cancel actions.
fails: A standalone action with no surrounding context to signal it's clickable — without hover cues (touch devices) or a nearby affordance, a ghost button can read as inert text.

claim: Set horizontal padding on a standalone button so the total width lands at roughly twice the button's height.
why: A 2:1 width-to-height ratio produces a shape that reads unmistakably as a button — wide enough to look pressable, not so wide it becomes a bar — and gives you a repeatable rule instead of eyeballing padding per label.
when: Standalone CTA buttons with short labels, especially paired primary/secondary actions.
fails: Long labels, where the text itself already exceeds twice the height — there the ratio is a floor, not a target, and you fall back to a fixed horizontal padding value.

claim: Present a primary and a secondary CTA side by side and differentiate them by fill weight, not by size or position alone.
why: Keeping both at the same dimensions and varying only the background lets the eye pick the primary action instantly while the secondary stays available.
when: Hero sections, dialogs, onboarding steps, and any moment offering one recommended action plus an alternative.
fails: When both actions are genuinely equal in weight, or when one is destructive and needs colour-based separation rather than emphasis ranking.

claim: Design one button component that renders identically with or without a leading icon, keeping height and padding constant across both.
why: If the icon is already sized to the line height, adding it changes nothing about the button's box, so a single set of tokens covers both variants and buttons stay aligned in a row.
when: Building a button in a design system or component library.

claim: Size the design system to the team's stage and surface area: for a small team shipping fast, ship a thin set of tokens and a handful of components you're willing to delete; only invest in exhaustive specification once the same patterns must hold across multiple products and large user populations.
why: The cost of maintaining a system scales with its specificity, and a startup's patterns change faster than documentation can keep up, so heavy systems become stale debt rather than leverage.
when: Deciding the initial scope and rigour of a new design system, or auditing whether an existing one is over- or under-built.
fails: Used as an excuse for permanent under-investment — a product that has grown into many surfaces and teams still needs the deeper definition, and staying 'lightweight' past that point produces drift.

claim: Build the system by explicitly defining the foundational layers first — spacing scale, type scale, colour roles, and interaction patterns — rather than by cataloguing screens you have already designed.
why: Codifying the underlying rules produces an architecture that new, unanticipated features can be built on; a catalogue of past screens only describes what already exists.
when: Starting a design system, or converting an existing ad-hoc UI into a systematic one.
fails: Rules get defined so far ahead of real product needs that the scale and patterns are guesses; foundations should be extracted from at least a few real screens.

claim: Treat the process of building the system as a deliverable in its own right: document the decisions and their rationale, and involve the people who will consume it, because the alignment produced during definition outlasts any particular component library.
why: The stated value is that developing the system matters more than the resulting artifact — the shared understanding is what lets a team expand coherently.
when: Any multi-person design or design-engineering effort where consistency across contributors is the goal.
fails: Process becomes the point and no usable artifact ships — the team debates tokens for months while product work stalls.

claim: Judge a design system by whether it gives the team a common vocabulary for describing and assembling UI, not by whether every screen looks identical; allow contextual variation where the product genuinely differs.
why: The purpose is shared language and communication efficiency, so uniformity is a side effect at best and a failure mode when enforced as a goal.
when: Reviewing designs against the system, or defending a system's value to stakeholders who equate it with visual sameness.
fails: Invoked to justify unconstrained one-off styling; variation still has to be expressible in the system's vocabulary.

claim: When a screen needs to depart from the system, make the departure explicit — name which rule is being broken and why — rather than letting it happen through inattention; unintentional deviations are defects, intentional ones are decisions.
why: Deliberate exceptions can be reviewed, documented, and later folded back into the system, whereas accidental drift accumulates invisibly and erodes the shared language.
when: Designing a high-stakes or unusual surface (marketing pages, onboarding, a flagship feature) where the standard components underserve the goal.
fails: Every deviation is declared 'intentional' as a rubber stamp — the discipline only works if the reasoning is actually stated and challengeable.

claim: Design a lightweight system to be disposable: keep components loosely coupled and avoid deep abstraction layers so that a pattern that stops working can be replaced quickly instead of being worked around.
why: Early-stage systems are stated to need to be quick to update and easy to scrap, which only holds if nothing else is tightly built on top of any single decision.
when: Building the first version of a system for a product whose direction is still changing.
fails: Applied to a mature system where downstream teams depend on stability — there, churn is more expensive than the wrong-but-stable pattern.

claim: Source every icon in a product from one icon pack or library rather than searching a general icon marketplace per-icon.
why: A single pack is drawn by one hand to one spec, so stroke weight, corner radius, grid, and optical density match automatically; assembling icons individually from a marketplace guarantees mismatches you then have to correct by hand.
when: Any interface needing more than one or two icons — nav bars, feature lists, settings screens, toolbars.
fails: The product needs domain-specific glyphs no single pack covers; then commit to one pack as the base and draw the missing icons to that pack's grid, stroke weight, and terminal style rather than importing a foreign one.

claim: Scale icon detail with icon size: at small sizes (roughly 16-24px) reduce to a single silhouette or a couple of strokes; only add interior detail as the icon grows to 48px and beyond.
why: Fine detail below the render size collapses into visual mud and reads as noise, while a large icon built from too few strokes looks empty and unresolved.
when: Choosing or drawing icons for a specific slot where the pixel size is already known.
fails: Using it as licence to add detail purely because there is room — a large icon can stay simple; the rule sets a ceiling on detail at small sizes, not a quota at large ones.

claim: Prefer the simplest icon that still reads as the concept; reject illustration-grade artwork used as an interface icon.
why: An icon is a wayfinding label, not a decorative asset — extra rendering slows recognition and competes with the content it is meant to point at.
when: Functional UI icons in navigation, buttons, list rows, and form fields.
fails: Contexts where the icon is the content — empty states, marketing feature cards, onboarding illustrations — where richer artwork is appropriate.

claim: Set icon size deliberately as a design decision rather than accepting whatever the source file exports at.
why: Icons dropped in at their native export size land at inconsistent optical weights next to each other and next to adjacent text.
when: Placing icons into an existing layout alongside type and controls.

claim: Accept a smaller, more limited icon library over a huge one when its coverage spans the common UI concepts you need.
why: Breadth of selection matters less than internal consistency; a constrained set removes the styling decision entirely and covers the standard vocabulary (search, settings, arrows, user, close) that most interfaces actually run on.
when: Picking an icon system at the start of a project.
fails: Icon-dense products — dashboards, editors, enterprise tools — where a thin library forces frequent custom drawing and a broader system is the better base.

claim: When one section has to carry several parallel messages, split it into a tab-style multi-section block where the visitor clicks a label to swap the panel content, rather than stacking every message as its own full-height section.
why: It compresses several competing pieces of content into a single screen's worth of vertical space while letting the visitor choose which one to read.
when: Marketing or product pages presenting 3–5 sibling items of equal weight — feature categories, audience segments, use cases.
fails: The content items are not siblings, or the visitor needs to compare them side by side — hiding panels behind clicks makes comparison and scanning impossible.

claim: Build the multi-section block in whichever orientation the content needs — tab labels running horizontally above the panel, or stacked vertically beside it — and treat the two as the same component rather than two different designs.
why: The same interaction pattern survives reorientation, so one pattern can be reused several times on a page without the page feeling repetitive.
when: A page needs the pattern more than once and you want visual variety without inventing a new component each time.
fails: Vertical label stacks with long labels or many items push the panel into a narrow column; horizontal labels break down past roughly five items or on narrow viewports.

claim: Default to click-only tab switching; only add automatic timed advancement if you are prepared to design and specify the timer, the progress indicator, and the pause-on-interaction behaviour.
why: Auto-advance multiplies the states and edge cases that must be designed and built, and the manual version delivers most of the value at a fraction of the cost.
when: You are choosing an interaction model for a tabbed section under normal time and budget constraints.
fails: The block is a hero carousel meant to be seen passively without interaction, where auto-advance is what surfaces content the visitor would never click.

claim: Design the full panel content for every tab before handoff — never ship a file with tab one complete and tabs two through four empty or duplicated placeholders.
why: The developer or client has no source for the missing states, so they either invent content or ship a broken section; the missing panels are real screens, not variations.
when: Any handoff of a component with multiple mutually exclusive content states — tabs, accordions, carousels, filtered views.

claim: Prefer flat, illustrative, or simple graphical treatments over photoreal 3D renders for product page visuals.
why: Render-heavy 3D reads as dated and expensive-for-its-own-sake in current software design, and it costs real production time and money to produce and maintain.
when: Choosing hero and feature-section imagery for a modern SaaS or software marketing site.
fails: The product itself is 3D, spatial, or hardware, where a render is the honest depiction of the thing being sold.

claim: Keep interface animation small in scope — element-level transitions, state changes, subtle reveals — but execute those few animations with precise timing and easing rather than dropping in defaults.
why: Restraint is a choice about scope, not about care; sloppy small animation is more noticeable than no animation because it happens right where the user is looking.
when: Adding motion to a software marketing page or product interface.
fails: Treating 'simple animation' as permission to skip the motion spec entirely, leaving timing and easing to the developer's defaults.

claim: Look for interactions beyond hover — click, scroll position, and tab selection are all triggers worth designing motion for.
why: Hover is unavailable on touch devices and is only one of several moments where a state change can be made legible through motion.
when: Specifying which moments in a page get animated treatment.

claim: Before styling a widget, check that every action button is something the underlying object can actually do; delete any action the real-world entity does not support and replace it with one it does.
why: A visually polished component that offers impossible actions breaks the user's mental model and signals the designer never thought past the aesthetics.
when: Designing UI for domain objects with real-world constraints — payment instruments, accounts, devices, documents.
fails: The object genuinely supports the action in some edge configuration, or you strip an action that exists for a less common but valid flow.

claim: Match data field labels to the object's actual semantics — a credit card surfaces minimum payment and due date, not a monthly fee.
why: Labels are the fastest thing a user reads; wrong ones make correct data misleading and hide the field the user actually came for.
when: Populating any data widget copied or adapted from a template built for a different object type.

claim: When a component type already exists as a well-solved product in the real world, copy its layout wholesale rather than inventing one, then re-skin it with your brand colours.
why: Familiar patterns carry recognition for free; the design work worth spending time on is the parts that are actually specific to your product.
when: Skeuomorphic or object-representing components — cards, tickets, boarding passes, receipts.
fails: The borrowed design encodes the source product's constraints or branding in ways that conflict with yours, or the copy is close enough to read as imitation.

claim: Fill a large empty surface by scaling the brand logo up past the component bounds and dropping its opacity so it reads as texture rather than content.
why: Big flat areas feel unfinished, but adding real elements adds noise; a low-opacity mark adds visual weight and brand presence at zero informational cost.
when: A component has a large solid colour field with nothing competing for attention — cards, hero panels, empty states.
fails: Opacity is high enough that the mark competes with foreground text, or the surface already carries data that needs contrast.

claim: When a widget shows a single instance of something a user could plausibly have several of, build the multi-item affordance — a scroll or pager — during the first pass.
why: Designing for one and retrofitting for many usually forces a layout rewrite; the scroll affordance costs almost nothing up front.
when: Widgets bound to collections that start at one — cards, accounts, connected devices, saved addresses.
fails: The entity is genuinely singular by system rule, where the affordance implies capability that does not exist.

claim: Treat the dashboard as a grid where importance maps to position: highest-priority widgets go top and left, lower-priority widgets fall down and right.
why: Reading order in left-to-right layouts starts top-left, so spatial position is the cheapest available signal of hierarchy.
when: Multi-widget dashboard layouts for left-to-right reading cultures.
fails: Right-to-left locales, or layouts where a deliberate focal element overrides reading order.

claim: Rank each widget's importance as you design it — a running tier list — instead of waiting until every widget exists to decide layout.
why: Layout decisions need relative priority, and assigning a provisional tier at creation time keeps you moving without locking the grid prematurely.
when: Designing a dashboard incrementally where the full widget set is not yet known.
fails: Early rankings are treated as final; tiers assigned before the full set exists need revisiting once everything is on the board.

claim: Zoom into an inherited or reference design at component level and audit its content before adopting it — surface appeal frequently hides content that makes no sense.
why: Portfolio-style concept work optimises for the thumbnail, so its labels and actions are often decorative rather than functional.
when: Using Dribbble shots, templates, or any concept design as a base for real product work.

claim: When nesting one rounded shape inside another, set the inner radius to the outer radius minus the padding between them (inner = outer − gap), so the two arcs stay concentric.
why: With equal radii, the visual gap between the two curves widens at the corners even though the straight-edge padding is uniform, which reads as sloppy spacing.
when: Any container-within-container pattern: card inside a panel, image inside a card, icon tile inside a button, screen inside a device frame.
fails: When the padding is larger than the outer radius, the formula yields zero or negative values; at that point pick a small radius by eye instead.

claim: Never reuse the same corner radius token for a child and its parent — the child's radius must always be smaller than the parent's by the padding amount.
why: Identical radii are what produce the swelling-corner artefact; the mismatch is a function of padding, not a style choice.
when: Building radius scales in a design system where nested surfaces are common.
fails: Elements that sit side by side rather than nested share a radius freely; the rule is only about containment.

claim: Skip the concentric-radius maths for pill shapes (radius = half the height); leave fully-rounded children fully rounded.
why: A pill's edge is equidistant from its center path all the way around, so nesting a pill in a pill already keeps the gap constant.
when: Pill buttons inside pill containers, avatars/circles inside circular frames, fully-rounded chips.

claim: Judge corner nesting optically as the final check — compare the corner gap to the edge gap by eye and adjust until they read the same, rather than trusting the number.
why: The formula is a starting point that only holds inside a limited range of gap-to-radius ratios; the goal is perceived even padding.
when: Large padding, unusual radii, or any case where the computed value looks wrong on screen.

claim: For a more refined corner, apply Figma's iOS corner smoothing (squircle) at maximum to all four corners so the curve eases in before the arc rather than meeting the straight edge abruptly.
why: The tangent transition between straight edge and arc is a visible discontinuity; smoothing tapers it and matches the corner language of Apple platforms.
when: Polish passes on large rounded surfaces — cards, app icons, sheets — where the corner occupies enough pixels to be perceived.
fails: The effect is nearly invisible at small radii or small element sizes, so it is not worth the effort or the export complexity there.

claim: Verify subtle corner treatments by stacking the treated and untreated shapes and looking at where their outlines diverge.
why: Differences too small to see in isolation become legible as a gap when the two versions are overlaid.
when: Evaluating any low-amplitude geometry change — smoothing, one- or two-pixel radius shifts, optical tweaks.

claim: Delete field labels from card content when the value's format or an icon already communicates what it is; keep the label only where two similar-looking values sit adjacent and could be confused.
why: Labels double the amount of text without adding information, and needing one is a signal the value's presentation is not self-evident; the exception is when two values of the same type are side by side and order alone won't tell them apart.
when: Compact cards showing common, recognisable attribute types — price, rating, counts, place names.
fails: Values that are ambiguous on their own (two dates, two prices, unfamiliar or domain-specific metrics), or where accessibility and form semantics require an explicit name.

claim: Before laying out a card, cluster its fields into semantic groups — identity, commercial terms, specifications, dates — and treat each group as one visual unit rather than positioning fields individually.
why: Users scan for a category of answer, not a specific field; adjacency and shared alignment let a group be read as a single chunk in one fixation.
when: Any card or record view carrying more than about four distinct attributes.
fails: Cards with too few fields to form meaningful groups, where grouping just adds arbitrary structure.

claim: Rank the groups by how much they drive the user's decision, then place the top-ranked groups first and demote the group that only matters after the decision is made to the bottom of the card.
why: Card real estate maps to attention; details that are only checked once a user has already accepted the other criteria are a poor use of the top of the card.
when: Listing and browse cards where the user is comparing many items and filtering down.
fails: Contexts where the 'late' field is actually the primary filter — a date-first booking flow, for instance, inverts this ranking.

claim: Give a card visual hierarchy by pairing related fields into two-line stacks and pushing one stack to the left edge and the other to the right edge of the same row, instead of stacking every field in one left-aligned column.
why: A left/right split creates a horizontal axis of comparison and fills the card's width, so two groups occupy the vertical space one column would, while opposing alignment separates the groups without needing a divider.
when: Cards with two roughly equal-weight groups, such as name+location versus price+rating.
fails: Very narrow cards or mobile widths where the two edges collapse together and the split reads as a broken column.

claim: Compress a set of small homogeneous specs into a single horizontal row and prefix each with an icon rather than a text label.
why: The icon carries the category meaning in a fraction of the width a label needs, so the specs cost one line instead of several and gain a scannable visual rhythm.
when: Short, countable specs with well-established icon conventions — bedrooms, beds, baths, guests, area.
fails: Concepts with no conventional icon, where an invented glyph is less legible than the word it replaced.

claim: Evaluate a card redesign by rendering the old and new versions side by side at the same size rather than judging the new one alone.
why: The improvement lives in the contrast; in isolation a redesign always looks acceptable, and the direct comparison is what exposes whether hierarchy actually improved.
when: Any iteration on an existing component.

claim: Treat a card that is merely readable as an unfinished draft: correctness of information is the floor, and the layout pass that adds hierarchy is a separate, required step.
why: A flat enumeration of true facts communicates everything with equal emphasis, which means it emphasises nothing and forces the user to do the ranking work.
when: Cards generated straight from a data model or API response shape.
fails: Dense data tables and admin tools where uniform, unranked rows are the point and users compare across rows rather than within one.

claim: Pick one base spacing unit — 4px or 8px — and make every gap, padding, and margin a multiple of it.
why: A single divisor removes arbitrary one-off values, so rhythm repeats across the interface and the whole layout reads as deliberate rather than hand-placed.
when: Any interface with repeated components; most valuable on dense, small-scale elements like cards, list rows, and form fields where a 3px inconsistency is visible side by side.
fails: Rigidly applying the base unit to large dimensions or to optical alignment problems (icon centring, text overhang) where the correct value is whatever looks right, not whatever divides evenly.

claim: Change your design tool's small-nudge increment to match your base unit (Figma: Preferences → Nudge amount, 10 → 8) instead of leaving the default.
why: Consistency breaks during small tweaks, not during initial layout; if the arrow key moves objects by a number that isn't a multiple of your unit, every nudge silently drifts elements off-grid.
when: As soon as you commit to a base grid — set it once per tool, before production work starts.
fails: Working across files or teams with different base units, where a global nudge setting fights the file you're currently in.

claim: Above roughly 100px, round dimensions to the nearest 5 or 10 rather than forcing multiples of 8.
why: The perceptual difference between 120 and 128 is negligible, so the strictness buys no visual gain while costing round, memorable numbers.
when: Large-scale measurements — container widths, hero heights, section blocks — where the value is not sitting next to a sibling for comparison.
fails: The large element must align to a column grid or stack flush with gridded children; there, breaking the multiple reintroduces the odd leftover gaps the system exists to prevent.

claim: If you do need large sizes to stay on an 8px system, jump in progressively bigger steps rather than adding 8 at a time.
why: Spacing perception is proportional, not absolute — an 8px step is a large relative change at 16px and an invisible one at 200px, so a linear scale wastes steps at the top end.
when: Building a spacing or sizing token scale that has to cover both component-level and page-level values.

claim: Audit spacing consistency by dividing the observed values by your base unit; any value that doesn't divide cleanly is the thing to fix.
why: It converts a vague 'this looks off' judgement into a mechanical check that can be applied without taste or debate.
when: Reviewing or handing off a component, or debugging a layout that feels untidy for no obvious reason.
fails: Intentional optical corrections will fail the check; exclude them rather than snapping them back to the grid.

claim: Separate the positioning wrapper from the styled surface: use an outer section purely for placement on the page, and an inner container div that owns the background colour, radius, and the animated dimensions.
why: An element that both anchors itself in page flow and animates its own size fights itself — scaling or expanding the painted surface shifts everything around it. Splitting the two lets the inner box grow freely inside a stable outer frame.
when: Building any component whose box will expand, collapse, or morph — nav bars, dropdowns, docks, expanding search fields.
fails: For a purely static block with no size animation, the extra wrapper is dead markup; also fails if the outer section is given its own padding or background, which reintroduces the coupling you were avoiding.

claim: Build interactive components outside-in: create the outermost wrapper first, then the styled container, then the interior element groups, then the leaf content — do not write leaf markup before its parents exist.
why: Animation targets are almost always ancestors of the content that moves. Establishing the containment chain first means each new child inherits a known parent to be positioned and clipped against, instead of being retrofitted later.
when: Hand-coding a component that will be animated or that has nested layout groups.
fails: Less useful when composing from pre-built components, where the nesting is already fixed by the library.

claim: Wrap each logical cluster of a nav bar's contents in its own named sub-container (a menu group, a links group) rather than placing icons and labels as direct siblings of the outer container.
why: Groups can be spaced, aligned, and faded as units, and can be animated on independent delays; loose siblings force you to target each item individually and re-derive their relationships in every rule.
when: Any horizontal bar with two or more distinct content zones.
fails: A bar with a single element — the extra grouping layer adds nothing.

claim: Name containers after the role they play in the component (nav-container, menu-container) rather than after their appearance or position.
why: Role names survive visual redesigns and let a reader infer the structure from the markup alone, which matters when the same class is later referenced by animation code.
when: Authoring class names for hand-built components.

claim: Set the surrounding page up first — background treatment, headline block, content below — before building the component you actually intend to animate.
why: An entrance animation is judged by how it lands against real page content; testing it on a blank canvas hides overlap, contrast, and timing problems relative to what the user is actually looking at.
when: Prototyping load or entrance animations for a page-level element.
fails: Not needed when isolating a component for a design system or Storybook-style demo, where the surrounding page is intentionally absent.

claim: Reuse the same structural pattern across every component in a demo set — same wrapper type, same nesting depth, same naming convention — so each new build starts from a known shape.
why: Consistent scaffolding removes decisions from the start of each component and makes shared animation and layout rules portable between them.
when: Building a series of related components in one file or project.

claim: When you lift a component from a design showcase or template, treat it as a starting layout only — re-map its colours, type styles, spacing, and states onto your own system before shipping it, and re-check its interaction behaviour separately from its appearance.
why: A component authored for someone else's product carries that product's palette and type decisions; dropped in unchanged, the mismatch is immediately visible, and the less visible problems (states, hierarchy, interaction) survive untouched because nobody looked past the colour clash.
when: Borrowing or copying a UI pattern from an external source into an existing product design.
fails: Not addressed in this chapter — it does not discuss when borrowing wholesale is acceptable (e.g. an early prototype, or a component from your own design system).

claim: Audit a UI element on two separate axes — how it looks and how it behaves — rather than judging it by appearance alone.
why: The narration explicitly separates 'UI' from 'UX' as the two things each element will be upgraded on, implying a visually acceptable component can still be functionally wrong.
when: Reviewing or improving any recurring interface component.

claim: In a grid of repeating cards, remove the per-card CTA button and make the entire card surface the link.
why: A button repeated across every card in a grid adds visual noise without adding information — the card already reads as one clickable object, so the button is redundant chrome.
when: Listings, feeds, article grids, product grids — any layout where the same card shape repeats and each card has exactly one destination.
fails: A card has more than one action or a specific, named action; also when the card must be reachable by keyboard or screen reader, where a bare clickable div gives no accessible affordance.

claim: Keep an explicit, labelled CTA button when the action is specific rather than generic navigation — e.g. 'Try it out', 'Add to cart'.
why: A named action tells the user what will happen; whole-card linking can only communicate 'go to this thing', so it cannot carry action-specific meaning.
when: Cards whose primary interaction is a commitment or a distinct verb, or single/featured cards rather than repeating rows.

claim: When a card is clickable but has no button, fade in an arrow or chevron icon on hover to signal that the card is a link.
why: Removing the button removes the visible affordance; a hover-revealed directional icon restores the signal without adding permanent clutter to the grid.
when: Pointer-driven interfaces using whole-card links.
fails: Touch devices, where there is no hover state — the affordance never appears, so it must be persistent or carried by other cues.

claim: For an image-overlay card, size the image to roughly 3/4 of the card height, run a dark gradient upward from the image's bottom edge over about the lower half, and place the text on top of it.
why: The gradient creates a controlled dark field beneath the text so it stays legible regardless of what the photo does in that area, while leaving the top of the image unobscured.
when: Editorial, media, or album-style cards where the image is the primary content and the label is secondary.
fails: Images whose lower region is already dark or busy in a way the gradient cannot rescue, or light-toned images where a dark gradient reads as a dirty smudge.

claim: Make the gradient's transition long and gradual rather than a short hard ramp — the smoother the falloff, the better the effect.
why: A short gradient reads as a visible band or hard edge sitting on the photo; a long falloff blends into the image so the darkening looks like part of the photograph.
when: Any scrim placed over photography for text legibility.

claim: Default to the separated layout (image above, text on an opaque background below) unless you control the image set; reserve the gradient-overlay card for curated imagery.
why: Text on a solid background is legible with any image whatsoever, while overlaid text depends on the tones and composition of each specific photo — so the overlay is the higher-risk choice.
when: User-uploaded, CMS-driven, or otherwise unvetted image sources.

claim: Set the card's paragraph/body text noticeably smaller than the title rather than near-equal, so the hierarchy inside the card is unambiguous.
why: Cards are small containers; if supporting copy competes with the heading, the eye has no entry point and the card reads as an undifferentiated block.
when: Any card carrying a title plus a description or excerpt.
fails: Dropping below roughly 12-14px, where the copy becomes unreadable rather than merely secondary.

claim: Apply consistent padding on all sides of the card content, and give the image the same treatment as the text — either inset it to match the text margins or bleed it fully to the card edge, not something in between.
why: Mismatched insets between the image and the text block are the most visible failure in a weak card; picking one of the two consistent options removes the ambiguity.
when: Any card combining media and text.

claim: Round the card's corners, and round nested elements (image, buttons) to match, to make the component read as friendlier and more contemporary than sharp 0px corners.
why: Corner radius is a tone signal — square corners read as utilitarian or dated, softened corners read as approachable.
when: Consumer-facing product and marketing UI.
fails: Dense data tools or brand systems deliberately built on hard geometry, where rounding dilutes the intended voice.

claim: When redesigning a card, fix the content and typeface before touching the layout — replace placeholder or weak copy with realistic text first.
why: Layout decisions like line length, text block height, and image ratio are all responses to real content; tuning them against filler means redoing them later.
when: Any component refresh or redesign pass.

claim: When you promote a CTA button higher in a card (next to the price rather than at the bottom), downgrade it to an outline/stroke style so it does not out-shout the price.
why: Position and visual weight both contribute to prominence; raising an element's position while keeping a solid fill gives it two boosts at once and lets it compete with the primary information.
when: Repositioning an action element into a more prominent slot in a compact card layout
fails: When the outline button is the only action on a page and needs to read as the primary target, or when contrast of the stroke style drops below accessible levels

claim: Replace neutral bullet dots in a pricing feature list with check marks, and use a contrasting negative mark for features the plan excludes.
why: A check communicates 'included' semantically instead of just delimiting a line, and pairing it with an exclusion marker turns the list into a comparison the user can reason about.
when: Feature lists inside plan or tier cards where inclusion versus exclusion is the decision the user is making
fails: Lists that are descriptive rather than inclusive — a check on a non-benefit reads as noise; also fails if excluded items are styled identically to included ones

claim: Give every pricing card an explicit plan name plus a one-line description of who or what it is for, above the price.
why: A price with no label forces the user to infer the tier from the feature list; a name gives them a handle to compare and refer to, and the description answers 'is this me?' before they read features.
when: Any multi-tier pricing layout where cards sit side by side

claim: If a headline price depends on billing terms, state the real recurring cost in small supporting text directly under the price.
why: Discovering a different price at checkout destroys trust; disclosing it in the card costs one line and preempts the feeling of being misled.
when: Annual-billing discounts, introductory rates, per-seat multipliers, or any price shown that is not what the user will actually be charged monthly

claim: Separate the price block from the feature block with a filled region — a low-opacity tint of the brand colour behind one section — instead of drawing a divider line.
why: A tinted area groups content by shared background rather than by cutting the card, which reads as two distinct zones while adding a touch of brand colour and less visual clutter than a rule.
when: Cards containing two functionally different content groups (offer vs. contents) that need visual separation
fails: When the tint reduces text contrast, or when many stacked sections each get their own tint and the card turns into stripes

claim: Write CTA labels as the action the user is taking rather than a generic noun or label.
why: Action phrasing tells the user what happens on click and reduces hesitation at the conversion point.
when: Any button that commits the user to a step in a purchase or signup flow

claim: Treat each edit as having a knock-on effect: after any change that alters an element's prominence, immediately re-check and rebalance the card's hierarchy.
why: The chapter shows a move that improves layout but breaks hierarchy, then repairs it in the same step — improvements are not independent of each other.
when: Iterative refinement of a dense component where elements compete for attention

claim: Order a pricing card as: plan name, short description, price, billing clarification, CTA, then feature list.
why: This sequence answers identification, cost, and commitment before asking the user to evaluate detail, and keeps the feature list as supporting evidence rather than the lead.
when: Standard SaaS subscription tier cards
fails: Enterprise or quote-based tiers where there is no price to lead with

claim: Do not give a chip your primary CTA colour — reserve that fill for actual buttons and use a neutral, tinted, or secondary colour for chips.
why: Colour is the main signal of action hierarchy on a page; if chips wear the primary colour they compete with the real call to action and the user can no longer tell what the page wants them to do.
when: Any interface where chips (tags, filters, breadcrumb segments, category pills) coexist with buttons on the same screen.
fails: A chip genuinely is the highest-priority action — e.g. a single selected state in a filter group, where a filled accent chip communicates selection rather than competing for the CTA role.

claim: Keep chips vertically shorter than the buttons in the same interface — a chip should read as a thinner horizontal pill, not a full-height control.
why: Height is the second hierarchy signal after colour; matching button height makes a chip indistinguishable from a button and misleads users about what will happen when they tap it.
when: Designing chips that sit near or alongside buttons in the same layout or design system.
fails: Touch-target minimums still apply — don't shrink a tappable chip below roughly 44px of hit area on mobile, even if the visible pill is shorter.

claim: Set a chip's vertical padding to one-half or one-quarter of its horizontal padding — e.g. 20px horizontal pairs with 10px or 5px vertical.
why: An asymmetric padding ratio is what produces the wide, thin silhouette that reads as a chip; equal padding on all sides produces a squat box that reads as a button.
when: Sizing any text-bearing chip, tag, pill, or badge.
fails: Chips containing an icon plus text, or multi-line content, where the ratio may need loosening to keep the icon from crowding the edges.

claim: Never hand-draw a chip as a fixed-size rectangle with a text layer on top — always wrap the text in an auto layout frame so the container derives its size from the label plus padding.
why: Chip labels are content-driven and vary in length; a hand-sized rectangle breaks the moment the label changes, while auto layout keeps padding constant and the shape correct across every label.
when: Every chip, in any Figma file, especially sets of chips with different-length labels.

claim: Build chips text-first: write the label, wrap it in auto layout, then apply fill and corner radius, then tune padding last.
why: Starting from the text means the container is sized by real content from the outset, so padding decisions are made against the actual label rather than an arbitrary box you later have to correct.
when: Creating a new chip component from scratch.

claim: Treat 'background too tight' and 'background too loose' as the two named failure modes to check a chip against — cramped padding looks unfinished, generous padding turns the chip into a button.
why: Chip quality lives almost entirely in the padding relationship; both errors are common and both are visible at a glance once you know to look for them.
when: Reviewing or critiquing an existing chip design.

claim: Round chip corners substantially — pill or heavily-rounded geometry, applied as a deliberate step after the fill.
why: A soft, rounded silhouette reinforces the lightweight, secondary read of a chip and further separates it from the more architectural corner radius typical of buttons.
when: Styling chips, tags, and filter pills.
fails: Design systems with a strictly rectilinear visual language, where chips must inherit the system's shared radius instead.

claim: Reach for chips when you need breadcrumb navigation or lightweight interactive affordances rather than inventing bespoke components.
why: Chips are compact, repeatable, and legible as 'small tappable thing', which fits path navigation and optional actions better than full buttons or plain links.
when: Landing pages and app screens that need wayfinding or optional, low-commitment interactions.
fails: Primary conversion actions, which need the weight and colour of a real button.

claim: Anchor compact component content to shared edges before adding filler or hiding actions.
why: Aligned text and controls establish an intelligible structure without extra separators.
when: Cards, sidebars, chat inputs and compact rows.
fails: Do not force decorative or intentionally asymmetric compositions onto every edge.

claim: Reorganize the avatar, buttons and content to establish a usable alignment line when the existing anchors leave the composition unresolved.
why: A new shared edge can resolve a layout while retaining useful controls.
when: A card has misaligned actions or awkward empty regions.
fails: Hide an action only when task priority justifies disclosure; alignment alone is not a reason to conceal it.

claim: Recheck row anchors after changing icon size or content height.
why: Larger icons can break the relationship between adjacent text rows.
when: A compact repeated component changes its proportions.
fails: Do not invent meaningless subtext simply to fill the gap.

claim: Replace explanatory text with a familiar diagram or visual cue only when it communicates the same meaning more immediately.
why: Adding explanations can increase reading work instead of clarifying the screen.
when: A familiar representation can carry information directly.
fails: An unfamiliar or ambiguous visual requires a label rather than relying on a delayed tooltip.

claim: Use conventional link styling and category chips to distinguish actionable content within a list.
why: Recognizable treatment conveys meaning and can expose direct interaction.
when: Links and editable categories occur inside otherwise uniform text.
fails: Do not style passive content as an editable control.
